head:
Finding · Physical fitness

Is our physical fitness really declining?

You hear everywhere that humans are less and less fit. This article checks what the measurements actually say, step by step, from the whole world down to what happens inside a body, then answers the only question that concerns you: what does it change for you, and what should you do?

The question

You have surely already heard the phrase: “people are less and less fit”. It comes up in newspapers, in public health speeches, in gym adverts. It is also suspect, for a simple reason: it is the kind of phrase people repeat without having checked it.

So we ask the question properly, with what the studies allow us to say and nothing more.

The question

Has human physical fitness really deteriorated over the past few decades, and why does it concern you personally?

It splits into two parts that are not equally difficult. The first is a finding: do people move less, and are they physically less capable than before? The second is a stake: if so, does it weigh on your health or your lifespan, or is it a subject for sociologists with no consequence for you?

We also need to distinguish two words that people constantly mix up. Physical activity is what you do: walking, training, carrying. Physical fitness is what your body is able to do: sustain a long effort, develop strength, get up from the floor. The first is asked about in a questionnaire. The second is measured with a test. Almost all the worldwide statistics on adults concern the first, because a questionnaire is easier to organise than a test. Knowing which of the two we are looking at, at each step, is half the work.

The demonstration goes from the most general to the most precise: all the adults in the world, then one country, then what physical tests measure, then the probable causes, then the link with health, and finally the objections that could bring everything down.

What is at stake

If the question had no consequence, it would not deserve an article. It has three, which affect you at different scales.

Your lifespan and your health. The follow-up studies, which we will see at step 5, link fitness level to the risk of death, with large differences. A 2016 American Heart Association statement even goes as far as asking for endurance to be measured at consultations as a vital sign, in the same way as blood pressure.13 Your doctor measures your weight and your cholesterol. Measuring your endurance is not routine, although it may be one of the best indicators of your condition.

Your independence. What is at stake is not only lifespan but what you will be able to do during those years: climb stairs, carry your shopping, get up after a fall. A test as simple as getting up from the floor with as little support as possible is linked to mortality in people aged 51 to 80, as we will see.14

Your training. If you train, the question affects you differently: knowing where the population average lies tells you how low a “normal” level has become, and therefore how poor a benchmark it is to compare yourself with the average.

There is also a collective stake. The WHO has set itself a global target of reducing inactivity by 2030. The authors of the largest recent study estimate that it will not be reached if the current trend continues.1 This cannot remain unanswered: if the trend is real, it is easier to correct early than late, and first of all at the level of each individual.
rest:
The demonstration

Six steps, from the widest picture to the finest. Each one builds on the previous one and refines a part of it.

Step 1
The widest view: how many adults move enough, worldwide

A team pooled 507 population surveys carried out in 163 countries and territories, covering 5.7 million adults. In each survey, adults reported their activity. The minimum used is the one recommended by the WHO: 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or an equivalent combination. The results are age-adjusted, which avoids the “the population is ageing” effect.1

Each decade, a larger share of adults does not reach the minimum

Reported activity, adults aged 18 and over, age-standardised. The 7.9-point gap is calculated (31.3 minus 23.4). Source: Strain et al., Lancet Global Health, 2024.1

What this means

In 2022, nearly one adult in three (31.3%) does not reach the minimum, compared with fewer than one in four in 2000. Women are more affected (33.8%) than men (28.7%). The share increased in 103 of the 197 countries and territories estimated, i.e. 52%, and among people aged 60 and over in every region.1 For you, this means that moving no longer happens by itself: movement has left everyday life (desk, car, screen) and now has to be decided on.

A single study is not enough to conclude. An earlier analysis, covering 358 surveys, 168 countries and 1.9 million people, found a different picture: 28.5% of adults insufficiently active in 2001 and 27.5% in 2016, a non-significant change.2 The two studies do not give the same starting level, so we do not compare their figures with each other, only their slopes.

Two worldwide studies, two slopes: only one sees the increase over the whole period

Same indicator (reported insufficient activity), two studies, two sets of surveys. The levels are not comparable between the two studies; the slope of the second is not statistically significant. Sources: Strain et al., 2024; Guthold et al., Lancet Global Health, 2018.1,2

What this means

The 2018 study does still see an increase in high-income countries, from 31.6% to 36.8% between 2001 and 2016, compared with 16.2% in low-income countries in 2016.2 The two studies therefore diverge on the global trend. The pages consulted do not explain this difference; the more recent one is based on more surveys and covers more years. The direction “more inactivity among adults in rich countries” is therefore the most solid. The size of the global increase is less so.

First result, then: adults report moving less, especially where life is most comfortable. But a global figure is an average of very different situations. We take a closer look at one country.

Step 2
One country up close: France, by sex and age

Santé publique France compares two national surveys of adults aged 18 to 74: ENNS in 2006-2007 (4,329 participants) and Esteban in 2014-2016 (3,864 participants). Again, these are questionnaires, so reported activity.3

In 2014-2016, 71% of men and 53% of women met the WHO guidelines. The change since 2006 is not the same for everyone: activity fell among women of all ages and rose among men aged 40 to 54. Screen time rose sharply among adults as well as children, although the page consulted gives no precise figure.3

Among young people, two different surveys give a snapshot. The Esteban survey estimates that about half of boys and a third of girls meet the guidelines, with no change since 2006.3 ANSES did another calculation in 2020, on 11 to 17-year-olds: 66% combine more than two hours of leisure screen time a day with less than 60 minutes of activity, including school sport, which it describes as a worrying health risk. Among 11 to 14-year-olds, 15.5% of girls reach 60 minutes a day, compared with 24% of boys.4

In France, women and adolescent girls are the ones who least often meet the guidelines

Two sources, two definitions: do not compare the top bars with the bottom ones. Both series describe a state, not a change. Sources: Santé publique France, BEH 2020; ANSES, press release of 23 November 2020.3,4

What this means

The decline is not uniform. In France, it appears among women; among men, reported activity is stable or rising depending on age. Among young people, the situation is poor without having worsened since 2006, and girls are further from the guideline than boys. For you: the average hides very different profiles, so what matters is your own measurement rather than a national average.

But all of this is still reported. A questionnaire measures what people say they do, not what their body can do. To see whether capacity itself has changed, we need tests where people run, cycle and jump.

Step 3
Physical tests: has capacity itself declined?

Young people's endurance. The reference is a review of 137 studies, which pools the results of 965,264 young people aged 9 to 17 in 19 countries (17 high-income, 2 upper-middle-income), between 1981 and 2014. All of them ran the 20-metre shuttle: you go back and forth between two lines, at a speed that keeps increasing, until you can no longer keep up. The result is used to estimate VO2max, the maximum amount of oxygen your body can use per minute, that is, your endurance.5

Young people's endurance dropped markedly in the 1980s and 1990s, then hardly any more

Physical measurement (20 m shuttle run, VO2max estimated by an equation). High-income or upper-middle-income countries only. Source: Tomkinson et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2019.5

What this means

Over the whole period, estimated VO2max fell by 3.3 mL/kg/min, i.e. 7.3%. A young person in 2014 therefore sustains an effort for less time than a young person of the same age in 1981. The decline affects 17 countries out of 19; Brazil and Japan improved slightly; France is among the countries with a large decline. It is large in boys and small in girls. The authors see in it a decline “suggestive of a notable setback in population health” (my translation). But the curve flattened around 2000: the level lost has not been regained, it has almost stopped falling.

Leg power. Endurance is only one capacity. Another analysis looks at the standing broad jump, which measures the muscular power of the legs: 10,940,801 young people aged 9 to 17, 29 countries, from 1960 to 2017. Over the whole period, performance improves by 1.73 cm per decade, which is negligible. It rises until the 1980s, slows in the 1990s, then falls from 2000 in most countries.6 In other words, young people's endurance stabilises after 2000 while this power declines. Neither indicator says that today's young people are “in great shape”.

Adults tested at work. A Swedish series reported by public radio covers more than 350,000 people aged 18 to 74, tested in the workplace with a six-minute cycling test, from 1995 to 2017. Average endurance fell by about 10% there, and the share of people with low fitness almost doubled, to about half of the working population studied.7 A conference abstract on 516,122 workplace health checks, from 2001 to 2020, points the same way: estimated fitness falls in all 12 occupational groups examined, by 9.4% in relative change among administrative and customer-service staff. The decline is more marked in men and in 18 to 34-year-olds, and the share with low fitness (below 32 mL/kg/min) increases most among manual workers and low-skilled jobs.8

What this means

When capacity is measured rather than reported, the direction stays the same: rather downward, over several decades, in young people as in employed adults. These two adult series perhaps come from the same workplace health checks: I cannot verify this, so I do not count them as two independent pieces of evidence. And they describe workers who were tested, not the whole population.

We now have a cross-checked finding: less reported activity, and a measured capacity lower than in previous generations, with nuances. It remains to understand why.

Step 4
The causes: what we know, and what we do not know

The most obvious candidate is work. An American analysis used Bureau of Labor Statistics data to reconstruct the physical effort required by occupations over five decades. In the early 1960s, about half of private-sector jobs required moderate physical effort. In the study published in 2011, only about 20% of them still do. Work-related energy expenditure fell by more than 100 calories per day over fifty years, and by 142 calories per day in men between 1960-1962 and 2000-2006.9,10

One American job in two required moderate effort; only one in five still does

United States, private sector. Classification by occupation, not by individual measurement; the authors consider their estimate rather conservative. Source: Church et al., PLoS ONE, 2011, via the Pennington Biomedical Research Center and Medical News Today.9,10

What this means

Movement was not only given up by choice: it was removed from daily life. A job that made you walk, carry and bend gave you activity every day without you thinking about it. That activity did not go away because you became lazy. It went away with the jobs. This is what makes voluntary training more important than before.

But we must remain cautious: this mechanism is proven for the United States and for work, not for every country or every capacity. And the studies on young people give puzzling results. In the review on endurance, the link with physical activity and with obesity is weak to negligible. The only notable link is a correlation with income inequality (Gini index) across 18 countries: countries moving towards equality have better trends. The authors note that reducing the gap between rich and poor could slow the decline, if the association is causal.5 Likewise, standing broad jump trends are not significantly linked to the available health or societal indicators.6 Screen time is rising in children as well as adults,3,4 but none of the studies read shows that it explains the decline in capacity.

The conclusion of this step is modest: one mechanism is well documented (the disappearance of physical work), several others are plausible without being demonstrated. We know better that fitness is declining than why.

Step 5
Why it concerns you: fitness and lifespan

We know what has changed. The next question is about the stake: does it matter? To answer it, we look at people followed for years and compare those who are fit with those who are less so.

Endurance. The largest study of this type, from the Cleveland Clinic, follows 122,007 patients who took a treadmill stress test between 1991 and 2014, for 8.4 years on average, with 13,637 deaths. Each person is classified into five fitness levels according to age. The elite group has a risk of death 80% lower than the lowest group. Among people aged 70 and over, the elite still have a 29% lower risk than the “high performance” group (risk ratio 0.71). The authors note that there is no ceiling to the benefit in their data.11

These patients are not a general population (a single centre, people who take a stress test), but the result is not isolated. A meta-analysis of 33 cohorts (102,980 people, 6,910 deaths) finds that one more step of fitness, measured in metabolic equivalents, goes with a 13% lower risk of death (relative risk of 0.87). Compared with high fitness, low fitness goes with a risk 1.70 times greater.12

Mobility. In a Brazilian cohort of 2,002 adults aged 51 to 80 (median follow-up 6.3 years, 159 deaths), a test in which you sit down on and rise from the floor with as little support as possible is scored from 0 to 10. The lowest-scoring group (0 to 3) has a risk of death 5 to 6 times higher than the group scoring 8 to 10, and each additional score point goes with 21% lower mortality.14

Behaviour. Among more than half a million adults in the United States and Europe, those who do leisure-time activity at one to two times the recommended minimum have a 31% lower risk of death than those who do none. At three to five times the minimum, the benefit reaches 39% and then levels off. Beyond ten times, there is no additional benefit, and no additional risk either.15

The first step matters most: going from nothing to something

Reported leisure-time activity, more than half a million adults, adjusted results (origin, education, smoking, medical history, alcohol, family situation, weight). The point at 10 times and more is placed at the previous level to show “no additional benefit”: the source does not publish a percentage for this group. Source: Arem et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 2015, via the National Cancer Institute press release.15

What this means

Three different measures (a stress test, a mobility test, an activity questionnaire), three different populations, and the same shape of result: the fitter people are, the lower the risk of death, with the greatest gain on leaving the lowest level. For you, this changes how you see effort: you do not need to train like an athlete to get the main benefit. And if you already train, doing more is not dangerous in these data.

On the comparison with smoking, we need to be precise. In the Cleveland Clinic study, smoking is associated with an adjusted risk of 1.41 and coronary artery disease with 1.29; the page consulted does not give the equivalent figure for low fitness, so I do not compare them figure against figure. The American Heart Association statement goes further: it links low fitness to a higher risk than that of the classic factors (smoking, hypertension, cholesterol, diabetes).13 This is a claim by experts, not a result I can recalculate here.

Step 6
The objections: what could bring all this down?

A demonstration that does not answer its objections is worth little. Here are five, from the most serious to the least serious.

“Illness explains everything.” This is reverse causation: a sick person has poor fitness and a higher risk of death, without one causing the other. It is the most serious objection to step 5. Cohort studies adjust for a large number of factors, but I have not read an analysis that excludes the first years of follow-up, and none of the pages consulted claims to have settled the matter. What argues the other way is my own reasoning, not a result: the decline in young people's endurance (step 3) concerns children and adolescents, in whom chronic illness is rare. It therefore cannot be entirely explained by illness.

“The people studied are not like everyone else.” This is selection bias. The treadmill study covers a single centre and patients who take a stress test. The mobility study covers a Brazilian clinic, with adjustment limited to age, sex and body mass index. The series of tested adults come from employees.11,14,8 The results are therefore solid for these groups and plausible elsewhere, no more.

“Fit people also have good habits otherwise.” This is confounding. The studies adjust for smoking, alcohol, weight, medical history, but you can never correct for everything. Association is not cause: none of the studies read demonstrates that improving your fitness makes you live longer.

“These are only questionnaires.” For adults, this is largely true: the worldwide and French figures are reported. But the physical measurements, which are rarer, point in the same direction (young people, employees). For France, the only adult figure read is reported.

“So is it a collapse?” No. Young people's endurance dropped markedly, then stabilised around 2000. The two worldwide studies diverge on 2001-2016. French men's activity is stable or rising depending on age. The word “collapse” does not hold; “a decline over several decades, very uneven” does. And gaps remain: I did not find a solid series on adult strength, nor measured data for low-income countries.

The answer to the question

Let us return to the question: has human physical fitness really deteriorated, and why does it concern you?

Yes, on average and in rich countries, but not everywhere, not continuously and not at the same speed. What is solid: the share of adults who do not reach the minimum activity has increased in high-income countries, and, according to the largest recent study, worldwide between 2000 and 2022. Young people's measured endurance fell by about 7% between 1981 and 2014. What is probable: a similar decline in employed adults, a link with the disappearance of physical work. What is not: a continuous global decline (two studies diverge), a current fall in young people's endurance (stable since 2000), a decline in adult strength (no series read), and the exact causes.

And it concerns you because fitness level goes with lifespan, including among the people aged 70 and over in the treadmill study. Causation is not demonstrated and the illness objection is not entirely lifted. But three types of measures (stress test, mobility test, questionnaire) point in the same direction, and the data read do not show any additional risk from training a lot. Even in the worst case, where fitness would only be a sign of good health, it would remain a useful, measurable indicator that almost nobody tracks. That is the conclusion to keep: your fitness can be measured, compared with a norm table, and worked on.

What you can put in place

What follows derives from the studies read, but these are not proven results: they are reasonable consequences.

  • Measure first, before changing anything. Take the test on this page and note your result with the date. It is your starting point: a figure you can compare over time, which an impression does not allow.
  • Aim for the minimum before anything else. 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, or a mix.1 This is where the measured gain is greatest (step 5). If you are not there, it is your only priority.
  • Replace the movement your job no longer gives you. Step 4 explains why activity is no longer automatic. Walking to work, getting up regularly, taking the stairs: these are decisions to make, with no study read putting a figure on their effect.
  • Retest under the same conditions. Same protocol, same time of day, same equipment. Every 8 to 12 weeks is a reasonable pace; this is a coach's advice, not a value from a study. A change of less than a few percent may be measurement noise.
  • If you have children, the ANSES thresholds give a benchmark: more than two hours of leisure screen time a day and less than 60 minutes of activity are considered a risk.4

Chest pain or abnormal breathlessness during effort justify medical advice before you train harder. The test described below this article gives a starting level; it does not replace a doctor.

What these studies do not show
  • The worldwide adult data are reported, not measured, and the exact level remains approximate.
  • Young people's endurance is measured in high-income or upper-middle-income countries. VO2max there is estimated by an equation whose standard error is 5.9 mL/kg/min (12.1%).5
  • The Swedish adult series come from a press report and a conference abstract, not from articles read in full.
  • The links with mortality are observed associations. No study read demonstrates that improving fitness lengthens life.
  • I have no solid series on adult strength and no data from low-income countries.

Frequently asked questions

Is it simply the ageing of the population?

No. The worldwide figures are age-standardised, and the endurance and jump measurements concern young people aged 9 to 17.1,5,6

If young people's endurance has stopped falling, is the problem solved?

No. It has almost stopped falling, but it has not gone back up: the level lost between 1981 and 2014 remains lost, and leg power has been declining since 2000 in most countries.5,6

Do you have to train a lot for it to be useful?

No. In the leisure-time activity study, the benefit is already visible at one to two times the minimum and levels off around three to five times.15

If I am healthy, is measuring my fitness of any use?

That is what the American Heart Association statement argues: measuring fitness improves risk classification, and estimating it is no harder than estimating blood pressure.13
